query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In dual‐phase refractory high-entropy alloys with a microstructure composed of coherent δ-lamellae and strengthening γ″ precipitates, the retention of high toughness depends on maintaining a fine, coherent dispersion of precipitates. Systematic increases in aging temperature/time that promote precipitate coarsening and loss of interfacial coherence will degrade toughness by allowing dislocation slip to localize and shear the δ-lamellae rather than promoting distributed plasticity.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory HEA processed to form a dual-phase microstructure with coherent δ-lamellae and fine γ″ precipitates (as produced by controlled thermo-mechanical processing similar to that in PMC10213035).
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of aging temperature and time to tune precipitate size, distribution, and coherency.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under engineering-relevant strain rates and temperatures (e.g., room temperature tensile tests up to strains of ~14% and service conditions) within the compositional and processing range typical of refractory HEAs.
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitate size and interfacial (coherency) quality between the δ-lamellae and γ″ precipitates that dictate dislocation interactions and local shear distribution.
generation.mechanism: Fine, coherent precipitates effectively pin dislocations and promote distributed, planar slip across δ-lamellae, delaying crack initiation and enhancing toughness. When aging conditions drive precipitate coarsening and loss of interfacial coherence, dislocations can shear larger lamellae more easily, leading to localized shear bands and decreased toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples aged under optimized conditions will exhibit high toughness with evidence of distributed dislocation slip and minimal local shear (~40% shear avoided). In contrast, overaged samples with coarsened, incoherent precipitates will show a reduction in toughness, characterized by prominent localized shear bands and earlier crack initiation compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The dual-phase refractory HEA processed under previously validated thermo-mechanical conditions (as in PMC10213035) that yield a microstructure with fine and coherent δ-lamellae and γ″ precipitates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold within the processing regime typical for refractory HEAs (e.g., controlled aging temperatures and times that do not induce unwanted phase transformations) and under mechanical loading conditions representative of demanding service environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between aging parameters, precipitate coherence, and toughness retention may vary with alloy composition and processing history. The threshold at which coarsening significantly degrades toughness is not firmly established and may require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of dual-phase refractory HEA samples using identical melt or powder metallurgy routes, then apply controlled aging treatments varying in temperature and time to deliberately tune precipitate size and coherency. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and HRTEM to quantify precipitate dimensions and coherence, and perform tensile tests (including measurements of toughness such as Charpy impact energy or ductility indicators) under standardized conditions.
measurements: TEM/HRTEM analysis for precipitate size and coherency
Quantitative analysis of dislocation structures and slip band formation via microscopy
Tensile testing to measure yield stress, ductility, and toughness
Fractography to assess the mode of failure (localized shear vs. distributed plasticity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples aged at higher temperatures/times exhibit significant precipitate coarsening and loss of coherence without a corresponding decrease in toughness (i.e., if toughness remains comparable to that of the baseline despite microstructural degradation), then the hypothesis that precipitate coherency is critical for toughness retention is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

frame.goal: Explain the mechanistic origin of toughness retention or degradation under demanding service conditions and define how controlled microstructural or compositional changes affect that behavior.
frame.limitation: Current models do not clearly decouple the influence of local elemental partitioning, phase stability, and microstructural heterogeneities on toughness in these alloys, leaving the exact mechanism ambiguous.

decision.trend: Early investigations (e.g., PMC5578249) focused on standard processing routes (casting combined with HIP treatment) in multi‐principal element alloys, where the appearance of secondary phases—such as HCP precipitates—was associated with extreme brittleness and loss of toughness. Later work (e.g., PMC10213035) moved toward sophisticated, step‐wise thermo‐mechanical processing designed to tailor dual-phase microstructures with coherent precipitates. These studies showed that controlled precipitation (e.g., δ‐lamellae and γ″ particles) enabled an unusual balance of ultrahigh strength with significant ductility. However, the experiments have been largely macroscopic or statistical in nature, leaving the individual influences of local elemental partitioning, phase stability, and microstructural heterogeneities on toughness retention only indirectly inferred.
decision.unsolved: The exact mechanistic origin governing whether toughness is retained or lost under demanding service conditions remains ambiguous. In particular, it is unclear how controlled changes in local elemental partitioning and precipitate coherency interact with phase stability and microstructural scale to dictate fracture resistance. The gap is the absence of an experiment that systematically varies one key processing parameter to decouple its effect on the microstructural features presumed to control toughness.
decision.lever: Systematic variation of aging temperature and time in a dual-phase refractory HEA (similar to the alloy processing in PMC10213035) to finely tune the precipitate size, distribution, and interfacial coherence.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend from macro‐scale processing to controlled microstructural tailoring and addresses the identified gap: decoupling the roles of local elemental partitioning and precipitate evolution on toughness. By precisely varying aging parameters, the experiment can establish a direct causal link between designed microstructural features and the retention (or loss) of toughness under simulated service conditions, thus testing the proposed mechanistic hypothesis.
